name: Narborough Bog
text: Your train passes close to Narborough Bog, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve of 8.5 hectares cared for by the Leicestershire and Rutland Wildlife Trust. It is mostly common reed growing on peat, with wet willow woodland, and is described as exceptionally rich in butterflies and moths.

name: Croft and Huncote Quarry
text: Your train passes near Croft and Huncote Quarry, on the train's {side}, where the quarry faces show igneous rock about 452 million years old. The site is protected for its geology, which helps tell the story of how the crust beneath central England grew.

name: St Mary in Arden Church, Market Harborough
text: Your train passes close to the ruins of St Mary in Arden, on the train's {side}, a church first recorded in 1220 and rebuilt in 1693. Every Easter Sunday the parish church choristers still sing the Easter Hymn over William Hubbard's grave there, as his bequest of a guinea a year asked in 1786.

name: Welford Road Stadium
text: Your train passes near Welford Road, on the train's {side}, the home of Leicester Tigers rugby club since it opened on September 10th 1892. It now holds 25,849 people.

name: Curve (theatre)
text: Your train passes near Curve, on the train's {side}, a theatre designed by Rafael Viñoly at the heart of Leicester's cultural quarter. It opened on November 11th 2008, with a main theatre of 970 seats and a studio of 350, and was officially opened by Queen Elizabeth II that December.

name: St Mary's Church, Sileby
text: Your train passes close to St Mary's Church in Sileby, on the train's {side}, founded around 1152. Its Gothic tower holds a ring of ten bells.

name: Barrow upon Soar
text: Your train passes Barrow upon Soar, on the train's {side}, known for a plesiosaur dug from a lime pit outside the village in 1851 and nicknamed the Barrow Kipper. The skeleton is on show at Leicester Museum & Art Gallery, and a sign of it stands on a roundabout in the middle of the village.

name: Taylor's Bell Foundry
text: Your train passes near Taylor's Bell Foundry in Loughborough, on the train's {side}, the world's largest working bell foundry, on this site since 1859. In 1881 it cast Great Paul for St Paul's Cathedral, a bell of more than 17 tonnes.

name: Brush Traction, Falcon Works
text: Your train passes close to the Falcon Works in Loughborough, on the train's {side}, where Henry Hughes was building steam locomotives by 1863. The Brush Electrical Engineering Company took the works over in 1889, and in the early 1900s built carriages for two of London's first tube railways.

name: St Giles' Church, Sandiacre
text: Your train passes near St Giles' Church in Sandiacre, on the train's {side}, which dates from the 11th century; its chancel was added around 1342. It is listed at Grade I.

name: Bennerley Viaduct
text: Your train passes near Bennerley Viaduct, on the train's {side}, a wrought-iron railway bridge known as the Iron Giant, completed in 1877 and 1,421 feet long. It carries a footpath and cycle route over the River Erewash, the boundary between Derbyshire and Nottinghamshire, and reopened for walkers and cyclists in January 2022.

name: Ironville
text: Your train passes near Ironville, on the train's {side}, a model village built around 1830 by the Butterley Company for its workers, beside the Cromford Canal. It was known for its large gardens, and gained a Mechanics Institute in 1846 and a church in 1852.

name: Crooked Spire, Chesterfield
text: Your train passes near Chesterfield's parish church, on the train's {side}, whose spire is both twisted and leaning: it twists through 45 degrees, and its tip leans about 2.9 metres off centre. Building of the church began in 1234.

name: Wingfield station
text: Your train passes right beside the old Wingfield station, on the train's {side}, designed by Francis Thompson and built for the North Midland Railway between 1836 and 1840. It is the only one of his 13 stations for that railway to survive as built, and after restoration finished in 2023 it is now a tea room and heritage centre.

name: Duffield Castle
text: Your train passes close to the site of Duffield Castle, on the train's {side}, a Norman castle whose stone keep was 31 metres across. It was destroyed in 1269, and its marked-out foundations were given to the National Trust in 1899, one of the Trust's earliest archaeological sites.

name: Derby Silk Mill
text: Your train passes near the Museum of Making, on the train's {side}, on the site of Lombe's Mill beside the River Derwent: built after John Lombe brought back details of Italian silk throwing machines from Piedmont in 1717, it was probably the first fully mechanised factory in the world. The museum reopened under its new name on May 21st 2021.

name: Midland Railway War Memorial
text: Your train passes close to the Midland Railway War Memorial, on the train's {side}, designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens and unveiled on December 15th 1921. It names the railway's men who died in the First World War: of some 23,000 who left to fight, 2,833 were killed.

name: Tutbury Castle
text: Your train passes near Tutbury Castle, on the train's {side}, a largely ruined medieval castle belonging to the Duchy of Lancaster. Eleanor of Aquitaine stayed there, and Mary, Queen of Scots, was held there as a prisoner.

name: Willington Power Station
text: Your train passes near Willington Power Station, on the train's {side}, a coal-fired station that closed in the 1990s. Most of it was demolished, but its five cooling towers, each 300 feet high, still dominate the skyline; peregrine falcons nested in one in the mid-1990s.

name: Pride Park Stadium
text: Your train passes near Pride Park Stadium, on the train's {side}, home of Derby County since it opened in 1997 in place of the Baseball Ground. It holds 33,597 people, and has hosted England against Mexico and Brazil against Ukraine.

name: British Celanese, Spondon
text: Your train passes close to the Spondon works of British Celanese, on the train's {side}. The company began in 1916, when the brothers Henri and Camille Dreyfus were invited to Britain to make cellulose acetate dope for the canvas skins of wartime aircraft. The name, adopted in 1923, is a contraction of cellulose and ease.

name: Toton TMD
text: Your train passes close to Toton Sidings, on the train's {side}, a railway depot that grew up to sort coal wagons from the coalfields. In the 1950s more than a million wagons a year passed through what was then the largest marshalling yard in Europe.

name: Nottingham Castle
text: Your train passes near Nottingham Castle, on the train's {side}, on Castle Rock, whose cliffs rise 130 feet. The Norman castle was pulled down after the Civil War, and the ducal mansion built in its place in the 1670s was burnt by rioters in 1831, then restored as a museum and art gallery in the 1870s.

name: Nottingham Tennis Centre
text: Your train passes near the Nottingham Tennis Centre, on the train's {side}, home of the Nottingham Open, played each June on grass as a warm-up for Wimbledon. The tournament was first known as the Nottingham Lawn Tennis Tournament, from 1887.

name: St Mary's Church, Attenborough
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Attenborough, on the train's {side}, whose chancel is recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086. Henry Ireton, Oliver Cromwell's son-in-law, was baptised there in 1611.

name: Attenborough Nature Reserve
text: Your train passes Attenborough Nature Reserve, on the train's {side}, made from gravel pits dug between 1929 and 1967. Sir David Attenborough opened the reserve in 1966, and the Nottinghamshire Wildlife Trust bought it in 2020.

name: Trent Viaducts
text: Your train crosses the River Trent on the Trent Viaducts, between Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire. The first bridge here was built in 1839 by Charles Blacker Vignoles for the Midland Counties Railway; a second was added beside it between 1891 and 1893.

name: Ratcliffe-on-Soar Power Station
text: Your train passes near Ratcliffe-on-Soar Power Station, on the train's {side}, with its eight cooling towers and a chimney 199 metres tall. It was the last coal-fired power station in the United Kingdom, and its closure on September 30th 2024 ended the country's coal-powered electricity.

name: Boots D10 building
text: Your train passes near the Boots factory's D10 building, on the train's {side}, designed by Owen Williams and built between 1930 and 1932 to make lotions and medicines in liquid form. Known as the Wets building, it is one of the most important Modernist buildings in Britain and is listed at Grade I.

name: GlaxoSmithKline Carbon Neutral Laboratory
text: Your train passes close to the University of Nottingham's Carbon Neutral Laboratory, on the train's {side}, the first of its kind in the UK. Built of wood, with a green roof and solar panels, it was paid for largely by a £12 million grant from GlaxoSmithKline.

name: Lenton Priory
text: Your train passes near the site of Lenton Priory, on the train's {side}, founded by William Peverel around 1102 to 1108 as a house of Cluniac monks. Its monks were mostly French until the late 14th century, and it was dissolved under Henry VIII.

name: Church of St Mary the Virgin and All Souls, Bulwell
text: Your train passes close to St Mary the Virgin and All Souls in Bulwell, on the train's {side}, built in 1849 and 1850 by Henry Isaac Stevens. It replaced an older church on the same site, perhaps from the 12th century, which was badly damaged by a storm in 1843.

name: St Mary Magdalene's Church, Hucknall
text: Your train passes near St Mary Magdalene's Church in Hucknall, on the train's {side}, where the Byron family kept their vault. Most of the Lords Byron are buried there, among them the poet, and his daughter Ada, Countess of Lovelace, rests there too.

name: Notts Golf Club
text: Your train passes near Notts Golf Club, on the train's {side}, whose course is known as Hollinwell after a holy well in the trees near the eighth fairway. The club was founded in 1887 and moved here in 1901.

name: Kirkby-in-Ashfield
text: Your train passes Kirkby-in-Ashfield, on the train's {side}, a town that began as a Danish settlement: its name means church town. In the old village by St Wilfrid's Church stands Kirkby Cross, what remains of a 13th-century village cross.

name: Kings Mill Reservoir
text: Your train passes Kings Mill Reservoir, on the train's {side}, made in 1839 when the Duke of Portland had 72 acres of farmland and an ancient mill pond flooded to supply water to the mills along the River Maun. A mill at Kings Mill is recorded in the Domesday Book.

name: Mansfield Museum
text: Your train passes right beside Mansfield Museum, on the train's {side}, which opened in 1904 in a tin tabernacle left to the town by the collector William Edward Baily, along with his collection. The present building replaced it in 1938.

name: Church of St Chad, Pleasley Vale
text: Your train passes near St Chad's Church in Pleasley Vale, on the train's {side}, first built in 1876 of painted timber by the mill owner Joseph Paget on the Derbyshire side of the River Meden. After a disagreement about how services were held, he had it taken down and rebuilt in brick and stone just across the river, in Nottinghamshire and a different diocese.

name: Shirebrook North station
text: Your train passes near the site of Shirebrook North station, on the train's {side}, on the Lancashire, Derbyshire and East Coast Railway from Chesterfield to Lincoln. The station has been demolished, and houses now stand on part of the site.

name: Creswell Model Village
text: Your train passes near Creswell Model Village, on the train's {side}, built in 1895 by the Bolsover Colliery Company for its miners to designs by Percy Houfton. Its 280 cottages stand in two circles round an oval green with a bandstand, and a tramway between the circles delivered coal to the houses.
